statement: The province should expand involuntary care for people with severe addiction and mental illness.

passages.title: 2024 Policy Platform 'Common Sense Change for BC' (prior general election, Rustad era; 2026 plank names reuse its chapters)
passages.quote:
Rehabilitation and enforcement go hand-in-hand. A life diverted from crime and
addiction is often a life saved. BC’s Conservatives believe in giving individuals every
opportunity to get their lives back on track, whether from crime, addiction, mental illness
or trauma.

passages.title: 2024 Policy Platform 'Common Sense Change for BC' (prior general election, Rustad era; 2026 plank names reuse its chapters)
passages.quote:
The Mental Health Act and involuntary care practices will be reviewed
 so BC will never have a repeat of Eby’s refusal to place high-risk individuals in
 secure treatment.
 ● Early mental health interventions in schools, which are vital to improving long-
 term mental health outcomes in children and adolescents. We will work to ensure
 schools have improved access to mental health professionals. Investing in mental
 wellness for our youth is investing in a healthier future.
 ● Supporting increased family involvement by increasing treatment
 opportunities that foster collaborative engagement between patients and families
 throughout the continuum of care.

passages.title: BC Hansard 2026-05-28 pm, Issue 188 (Komoks Treaty Act third reading, Conservative speeches)
passages.quote: They established a rapid access addiction phone line, providing free same-day access to medication-assisted treatment. That program is helping over 22,000 people per month. In addition, the budget includes money for involuntary care beds for people who cannot ask for help for themselves but clearly need the assistance — 100 beds between two locations in Surrey and Prince George. I look forward to making an announcement soon about those sites.

passages.title: BC Hansard 2026-04-13 pm, Issue 150 (DRIPA repeal debate; Halford, McInnis, Doerkson)
passages.quote: Somebody that is a young single mother that is struggling to get by and needs to access supportive housing to be able to shelter themselves and their children or a senior on a fixed income that needs to access supportive housing for shelter is very different from somebody that needs to access supportive housing because they have a brain injury or they’re suffering from a severe mental illness or they’re struggling with substance use but they don’t want to go to treatment or they haven’t been able to access treatment, which is quite commonly the case.

passages.title: Hansard — Feb 18 2026 Afternoon, Issue No. 118
passages.quote: Until we flip that around, this problem will continue to get worse. The costs will continue to increase, a decision that we all will have to live with unless we make this fundamental paradigm shift in getting the support up front. We could have a lot less involuntary care. We could have a lot less in the way of mental health crises if we actually put the resources in up front.

passages.title: BC Hansard 2026-05-28 pm, Issue 188 (Komoks Treaty Act third reading, Conservative speeches)
passages.quote: We see that our crime numbers are coming down across the province, which is positive. They’re not where we want them. We want them even lower. There are street disorder issues that are not recorded in the crime statistics and that we also need to address, and we have involuntary care initiatives to support those who are really struggling in our streets on this.

passages.title: BC Hansard 2026-04-13 pm, Issue 150 (DRIPA repeal debate; Halford, McInnis, Doerkson)
passages.quote: The bill complements other work that is underway, including increasing health system capacity through increased funding through Budget 2026; intensive mental health and addictions treatment, including increased funding through Budget 2026; complex care housing, staffing and service delivery models in supportive housing; and building safety, air quality and environmental health in supportive housing. These initiatives and other related initiatives are being advanced through other policy and funding mechanisms. Bill 11 focuses on ensuring that the RTA doesn’t prevent timely safety interventions while broader system work continues.

passages.title: Hansard — Feb 18 2026 Afternoon, Issue No. 118
passages.quote: There are simply not the resources being made available for the wraparound care, and that leads to expansion and expanded use of involuntary treatment. It was deeply concerning to see a public servant mentioned by name in the budget twice, an indication perhaps of the capture of a single way of thinking that has overtaken this government. That is a very big concern for us because we know that this is an issue that needs to be dealt with in a variety of ways and in a variety of parts of the province without a single-minded, one-size-fits-all approach.
